source_text: Adhuc adiciam illam quoque partem in qua dum haereticus quasi oculo quodam gaudet proprio, ueritatis et luminis amisso, totam caecitatem sui agnoscat erroris. identidem enim et frequenter opponit quia dictum sit: sano tempore uobiscum sum, et non agnoscitis me? Philippe, qui uidit me, uidit et patrem. sed quod non intellegit, discat. culpatur Philippus, et iure quidem meritoque, quia dixerit: domine, ostende nobis patrem, et sufficit nobis. quando enim ex Christo aut audierat istud aut didicerat, quasi esset pater Christus, cum contra magis, quod filius esset, non quia pater, frequenter audisset, et saepe didicisset? quod enim dixit dominus, s me cognouistis, et patrem meum cognouistis, et a modo nostis illum, et uidistis illum, non sic dixerat ut se patrem uellet intellegi, sed quoniam qui penitus et plene et cum tota fide et tota religione accessit ad dei filium, omnibus modis per ipsum filium, in quem sic credit, ad patrem peruenturus sit, eundemque uisurus. nemo enim, inquit, potest uenire ad patrem nisi per me, et ideo ad patrem deum non tantum uenturus est, et cogniturus ipsum patrem, sed etiam sic tenere debet, atque ita animo ac mente praesumere, quasi iam nouerit patrem pariter et uiderit. Saepe enim scriptura diuina, quae nondum facta pro factis annuntiat, quia sic futura sunt, et quae omnibus modis fieri habent, non quasi futura sint, praedicat, sed quasi facta sint, narrat. denique cum nondum temporibus Isaiae prophetae Christus natus fuisset, quia puer, aiebat, natus est nobis; et cum nondum accessum esset ad Mariam, e accessit ad propheten, dicebat, e concepit, et peperit filium. et cum nondum sinum patris Christus exposuisset, referebat: e uocabitur nomen eius magni consili angelus. et cum nondum fuisset passus, guas? outs, pronuntiabat, ad iugulationem adductus est. et cum adhuc crux nusquam esset, aiebat: Tota die expandi manus meas ad populum non credentem., et cum nondum iniuriose potatus fuisset, s7fz, ait, mea potauerunt me aceto. et cum spoliatus adhuc non fuisset, dicebat, super uestem meam miserunt sortem: et dinumerauerunt ossa mea: effoderunt manus meas et pedes. prouidens enim scriptura diuina pro factis dicit, quae futura scit, et pro perfectis dicit, quae futura habet, quae sine dubitatione uentura sunt. et ideo dominus in praesenti loco dicebat: a modo nostis illum, et uidistis. dicebat enim uisum iri ab eo patrem, quisquis filium secutus fuisset; non quasi filius ipse esset pater uisus, sed quod praemium consecuturus esset, quisquis illum sequi et discipulus eius esse uoluisset, ut uidere patrem posset. nam et imago est dei patris, ut his etiam illud accedat, quoniam sicut pater operatur, ita operatur et filius, et imitator est filius omnium operum paternorum; ut perinde habeat unusquisque, quasi iam uiderit patrem, dum eum uidet qui inuisibilem patrem in omnibus operibus semper imitatur. Ceterum si ipse pater est Christus, quomodo confestim adicit et dicit: gud credit in me, opera quae ego facio et ipse Faciet, et maiora his faciet, quia ego ad patrem uado? et adhuc subnectit: si diligitis me, praecepta mea seruate: et ego rogabo patrem, et alium aduocatum dabit uobis. post quae etiam illud subnectit: s quis me diligit, sermonem meum custodiet: et pater meus diliget illum, et ad eum ueniemus, et mansionem apud illum Jaciemus. nec non etiam subdidit illud quoque: aduocatus autem ille spiritus sanctus, quem missurus est pater, ille uos docebit et commemorabit- omnia quaecumque dixero. praemittit adhuc istum locum, quo ostendat se esse filium, et merito subdidit, et dicit: s me diligeretis, gauderetis, quia eo ad patrem: quia pater maior me est. quid autem cum etiam ila subnectit: ego sum uitis uera, et pater meus agricola: omne sarmentum in me non afferens fructum tollit illud, et omne fructtSerum purgat, ut fructum ampliorem ferat? instat adhuc et adicit: sicut dilexit me pater, et ego dilexi uos; manete in mea caritate; si mandata mea seruaueritis, manebitis in mea caritale, sicut ego patris mandata seruaui, et maneo in eius caritate. adhuc ingerit, et dicit: dixi autem uos amicos, quia omnia quae audiui a patre meo, nota uobis feci. aggregat etiam hoc: sed haec omnia facient uobis propter nomen meum, quia ignorant eum qui me misit. Haec ergo numquam post illa euidenter illum non patrem sed filium esse testantia dominus subdidisset, si aut patrem se esse meminisset, aut patrem se uellet intellegi. nisi quoniam ut illud exprimeret, perinde unumquemque iam habere debere, dum imaginem dei patris per filium uidet, atque si uiderit patrem—quandoquidem unusquisque credens in filium exerceatur in imaginis contemplatione, ut assuefactus ad diuinitatem uidendam imagine proficere possit et crescere usque ad dei patris omnipotentis perfectam contemplationem,—et quoniam, qui hoc animo ac mentecombiberit et de omnibus sic futurum esse crediderit, patrem, quem uisurus sit, quasi iam quodammodo uiderit et hic iam sic habeat, quasi teneat, quod habiturum se pro certo sciat. Ceterum, si ipse pater fuisset, quid quasi futurum praemium repromittebat, quod iam praestiterat et dederat? nam quoniam dicit: beati mundo corde, quia ipsi deum uidebunt, polliceri deprehenditur contemplationem et aspectum patris. ergo nondum dederat: cur enim repromitteret, si iam dedisset? dederat enim, si pater esset; uidebatur enim, et contingebatur. quando autem, dum contingitur ipse Christus et uidetur, repromittit tamen et dicit, quoniam qui mundo fuerit corde, deum uidebit, hoc ipso probat patrem se non esse, qui tunc praesens cum uideretur repromittebat, quod patrem uisurus esset quisquis mundo corde fuisset. erat ergo repromittens haec non pater sed filius; quia qui filius erat, quod uideri habebat repromittebat: cuius repromissio superuacua fuisset, nisi filius fuisset. cur enim repromittebat mundis ut uiderent patrem, Si iam tunc qui praesentes erant, patrem Christum uidebant? sed quia filius erat, non pater, merito et filius, quia imago dei, tunc uidebatur, et pater, quia inuisibilis, mundis corde, ut uideretur, repromittitur et notatur. Haec igitur satis sit etiam aduersus istum haereticum dictasse, pauca de multis. campus enim, et quidem latus ac fusus, aperietur, plenius haereticum istum si agitare uoluerimus; quandoquidem duobus istis locis quibusdam effossis luminibus orbatus, totus sit in doctrinae suae caecitate superatus.
pass_a_gloss: I will also add that part in which, while the heretic, as it were, rejoices with his own eye, having lost the truth and light, may recognize the total blindness of his error. For he frequently opposes the fact that it was said: I am with you in healthy times, and you do not recognize me? Philip, who saw me, also saw the Father. But what he does not understand, let him learn. Philip is blamed, and rightly and deservedly so, because he said: Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us. For when did he hear or learn from Christ that Christ was the Father, since, on the contrary, he heard and learned more frequently that Christ was the Son, not the Father? For what the Lord said, If you have known me, you have also known my Father, and from now on you know him, and you have seen him, he did not say in order to be understood as the Father, but because whoever approaches the Son of God with total faith and religion will come to the Father through the Son, and will see him. For no one, he says, can come to the Father except through me, and therefore, one will not only come to the Father and know him, but also must hold and presume in mind and spirit as if one already knows and sees the Father. For divine scripture often announces what has not yet been done as if it were already done, because it will be done, and it predicts what will happen in every way, not as if it were going to happen, but as if it had already happened. Finally, when Christ had not yet been born in the time of the prophet Isaiah, it was said: A child has been born to us, and before he had come to Mary, it was said to the prophet: She has conceived and given birth to a son. And when Christ had not yet revealed the bosom of the Father, it was said: His name will be called Angel of great counsel. And when he had not yet suffered, it was announced: He was led to slaughter. And when the cross did not yet exist, it was said: I have stretched out my hands all day to a disobedient people. And when he had not yet been given vinegar to drink, it was said: They gave me vinegar to drink. And when he had not yet been stripped, it was said: They cast lots for my clothing, and they numbered my bones, and they pierced my hands and feet. For divine scripture speaks of what will be done as if it were already done, and of what will be perfected as if it were already perfect, because it knows what will happen without a doubt. And therefore the Lord said in this place: From now on you know him, and you have seen him, because he said that the Father would be seen by whoever followed the Son, not because the Son himself is the Father, but because whoever follows the Son and wants to be his disciple will receive the reward of seeing the Father. For the Son is the image of God the Father, so that it may be added that just as the Father works, so also the Son works, and the Son is the imitator of all the Father's works, so that each person may have it as if they had already seen the Father, while seeing the one who always imitates the invisible Father in all his works. But if Christ himself were the Father, how could he immediately add and say: He who believes in me will do the works that I do, and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father? And he also adds: If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another advocate. And after this, he also adds: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and we will make our dwelling with him. And he also adds: The advocate is the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send, and he will teach you and remind you of all that I have said. He anticipates this place to show that he is the Son, and rightly adds and says: If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than me. And what about when he also adds: I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer, and every branch that does not bear fruit in me will be taken away, and every fruitful branch will be purified, so that it may bear more fruit? He also adds: As the Father loved me, so I have loved you, remain in my love, if you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, just as I have kept the Father's commandments and remain in his love. He also says: I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all that I heard from my Father. He also adds: They will do all this to you on account of my name, because they do not know the one who sent me. Therefore, the Lord would not have added these things, which clearly show that he is not the Father but the Son, if he had remembered that he was the Father or wanted to be understood as the Father. But rather, he wanted to express that each person should have it as if they had already seen the Father, while seeing the image of God the Father through the Son, and as if they had seen the Father, since each believer in the Son is exercised in the contemplation of the image, so that, having become accustomed to seeing the divinity through the image, they may progress and grow until they reach the perfect contemplation of God the Father Almighty. But if Christ himself were the Father, what reward would he promise as if it were going to happen, when he had already given and provided it? For since he says: Blessed are the pure of heart, for they will see God, he is found to promise the contemplation and vision of the Father. Therefore, he had not yet given it, why would he promise it if he had already given it? He would have given it if he were the Father, for he would have been seen and touched. But when Christ, while being touched and seen, still promises and says that whoever is pure of heart will see God, he proves by this that he is not the Father, who, being present and visible, promises what he will see. Therefore, it was not the Father but the Son who was making these promises, because the Son, who had something to be seen, was making promises, and his promise would have been unnecessary if he were not the Son. Why would he promise the pure of heart that they would see the Father, if those who were present were already seeing the Father, Christ? But because he was the Son, not the Father, and rightly so, since he is the image of God, he was visible, and the Father, being invisible, is promised to the pure of heart, so that he may be seen. These things, then, are enough to have been said against this heretic, even if only a few of many things. For if we wanted to discuss this heretic further, a wide and extensive field would be opened, since, having been blinded by the removal of two passages, he is completely overcome by the blindness of his doctrine.

pass_b_english: I will also add that other part in which the heretic, as it were rejoicing with his own eye after losing the truth and the light, may recognize the total blindness of his error. For he repeatedly and frequently objects that it was said: 'I have been with you for so long a time, and you do not know me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). But what he does not understand, let him learn. Philip is blamed, and rightly and deservedly so, because he said: 'Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.' For when had he ever heard or learned from Christ that Christ was the Father, since, on the contrary, he had heard and learned more frequently that Christ was the Son, not because he was the Father? For what the Lord said — 'If you have known me, you have also known my Father, and from now on you know him and have seen him' — he did not say so that he himself might be understood as the Father, but because whoever approaches the Son of God with total faith and total religion, in every way through that Son in whom he so believes, is going to come to the Father and will see him. For no one, he says, can come to the Father except through me (John 14:6), and therefore one is not only going to come to God the Father and know him, but also must hold and presume in mind and spirit as if he already knows the Father and has seen him. For divine Scripture often announces things not yet done as if they were already done, because they are going to be so, and it declares things that must happen in every way, not as if they were going to happen, but as if they had already happened. Finally, when Christ had not yet been born in the times of the prophet Isaiah, it was said: 'For a child has been born to us' (Isaiah 9:6); and when he had not yet come to Mary, it was said to the prophet: 'Behold, she has conceived and will bear a son' (Isaiah 7:14); and when Christ had not yet revealed the bosom of the Father, it was reported: 'His name will be called Angel of Great Counsel'; and when he had not yet suffered, it was proclaimed: 'He was led to slaughter' (Isaiah 53:7); and when the cross did not yet exist anywhere, it was said: 'All day long I have stretched out my hands to a disobedient people' (Isaiah 65:2; Romans 10:21); and when he had not yet been insultingly given drink, it was said: 'They gave me vinegar to drink' (Psalm 69:21); and when he had not yet been stripped, it was said: 'They cast lots for my garment' (Psalm 22:18), 'They numbered my bones' (Psalm 22:17), 'They pierced my hands and my feet' (Psalm 22:16). For divine Scripture, foreseeing, speaks of future things as done, because it knows they will come to pass, and of future perfections as perfect, which are certainly going to come. And therefore the Lord said in this present place: 'From now on you know him and have seen him.' For he said that the Father would be seen by whoever had followed the Son; not as if the Son himself were the Father seen, but because whoever would follow the Son and wished to be his disciple would receive the reward of being able to see the Father. For the Son is also the image of God the Father (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3), so that this may be added: just as the Father works, so the Son also works, and the Son is the imitator of all the Father's works; so that each one may have it as if he had already seen the Father, while he sees the one who always imitates the invisible Father in all works. But if Christ himself is the Father, how does he immediately add and say: 'Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father' (John 14:12)? And he still adds: 'If you love me, keep my commandments: and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate' (John 14:15–16). And after these he also adds: 'If anyone loves me, he will keep my word: and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him' (John 14:23). Nor does he fail to add that also: 'But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you and remind you of all that I have said' (John 14:26). He premises that place to show that he is the Son, and rightly adds and says: 'If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I am going to the Father: for the Father is greater than I' (John 14:28). What, then, when he also adds: 'I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser: every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that bears fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit' (John 15:1–2)? He presses on and adds: 'As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you; abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love' (John 15:9–10). He further introduces and says: 'I have called you friends, because all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you' (John 15:15). He gathers also this: 'But they will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know the one who sent me' (John 15:21). These things, therefore, which clearly testify that he is not the Father but the Son, the Lord would never have added after those earlier words, if he had either remembered that he was the Father or wanted to be understood as the Father. Unless it was so that he might express that each one ought to have it as if he already held the Father, while seeing the image of God the Father through the Son, and as if he had seen the Father — since each one believing in the Son is exercised in the contemplation of the image, so that, having become accustomed to seeing the divinity through the image, he may progress and grow unto the perfect contemplation of God the Father Almighty — and because whoever drinks this in with mind and spirit and believes that all these things will be so, will have the Father whom he is going to see as if he had already seen him and already holds him here, as if he possesses what he knows he will certainly possess. But if he himself had been the Father, what reward would he promise as if it were future, which he had already granted and given? For since he says: 'Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God' (Matthew 5:8), he is caught promising the contemplation and vision of the Father. Therefore he had not yet given it: for why would he promise it if he had already given it? He would have given it if he were the Father; for he would have been seen and touched. But when Christ, while being touched and seen, still promises and says that whoever is pure in heart shall see God, this very fact proves that he is not the Father, who, being present while he was seen, was promising that whoever was pure in heart would see the Father. Therefore it was the Son, not the Father, who was promising these things; because the Son, who had something to be seen, was promising it: a promise that would have been superfluous unless he were the Son. For why would he promise the pure in heart that they would see the Father, if those who were present at that time were already seeing Christ the Father? But because he was the Son, not the Father, rightly the Son, because he is the image of God, was then visible, and the Father, because invisible, is promised and marked out to the pure in heart, that he may be seen. These things, then, are enough to have been said even against this heretic — a few things out of many. For a field, and indeed a broad and spread-out one, would be opened if we should wish to engage this heretic more fully; since, deprived of the light by two passages having been dug out, he is entirely overcome in the blindness of his doctrine.

The translation preserves the distinction between the Son being visible and the Father being invisible.
